subtype: Approach: runs a short team pre-mortem before a client demo [Thinking]
passage: The afternoon before the client demo in a Lisbon office, Ines handed out sticky notes and said, 'Write privately: it's tomorrow at ten, and the demo has failed. Why?' Six people wrote in silence for three minutes and folded their notes. Ines read them aloud without names. The confident planners had listed the projector, running late and too many slides. Freya, who rarely spoke in meetings, had written that the sample data took four minutes to load, and someone else added that the login page failed on the client's network. Nobody had mentioned either. Ines wrote both at the top of the board. By evening Freya had saved the sample data locally, and another colleague tested the login on a guest network.

qa.q: How many minutes did the team write in silence?
qa.a: They wrote in silence for three minutes.

qa.q: What might Freya have felt about speaking up in meetings, and how did the notes help?
qa.a: Freya probably felt hesitant, since Freya rarely spoke in meetings, and writing privately took away that pressure.

qa.q: What other step could the team take about the login risk?
qa.a: The team could ask the client beforehand which network and login they will use, since it answers the question before the demo.

qa.q: How might the confident planners have felt when the notes were read out?
qa.a: They were probably surprised and a little humbled, since nobody had mentioned the data or login risks.

grounding: Shows a team lead asking each colleague to write privately why the demo would fail, and quiet members raising data-loading and login risks the confident planners missed.

subtype: Approach: runs a short team pre-mortem before a client demo [Thinking]
passage:
The client demo was at ten the next morning. At six in the evening, in the small meeting room on the fourth floor, Dhruv handed out yellow slips.
"Imagine it's tomorrow at eleven and the demo went badly," he said. "Write down why. Don't sign it. Nobody talk yet."
The two senior developers wrote quickly and pushed their slips across. Mridul, who had joined three months ago and rarely spoke in meetings, wrote for a long time.
Dhruv read them aloud. The seniors had written "client asks for a feature we don't have" and "projector fails". Then Mridul's: "Dashboard takes forty seconds to load with real data. Login breaks if the client uses their office single sign-on."
The room went quiet. Nobody had tested either.
"Okay," Dhruv said. "Two things tonight. Mridul, can you show me the login problem first?"
Mridul nodded, cheeks a little pink.

qa.q: How long did Mridul say the dashboard takes to load with real data?
qa.a: Mridul wrote that it takes forty seconds to load with real data.

qa.q: What might Mridul's pink cheeks at the end suggest?
qa.a: Mridul may feel shy and a little proud at being taken seriously in front of the seniors.

qa.q: Why did writing silently work better than an open discussion here?
qa.a: It let a quiet newer member raise real risks without having to speak over confident seniors, so the two biggest problems came out in time.

qa.q: How might the client experience the demo if nobody had written the slips?
qa.a: The client might have waited forty seconds for a dashboard or been unable to log in, which could damage their trust in the team.

grounding: It shows a team lead asking colleagues to write privately why a demo might fail, so a quiet member raises loading and login risks others missed.

subtype: Approach: runs a short team pre-mortem before a client demo [Thinking]
passage:
Hi Parul,
Quick update before tomorrow's demo for the hospital client, and something I learned today.
At four, I asked the team to spend ten minutes writing, on their own, why tomorrow might go wrong. No discussion, no names. My thinking was simple: in our stand-ups the same three people talk, and I have no idea what the others are worried about.
I expected nothing new. Instead, Ritu, who has hardly said a word in two months, wrote that the patient records load slowly after the first hundred rows. Another slip said the login page times out on the hospital's network.
Neither of those had come up in any meeting. The confident planners, me included, had focused on the slides.
We're testing both tonight. If the load problem is real, we'll demo with a smaller sample and say so honestly.
Sachin

qa.q: At what time did Sachin ask the team to write down their worries?
qa.a: At four, Sachin asked the team to spend ten minutes writing on their own.

qa.q: What was Sachin feeling on reading the slips?
qa.a: Sachin was surprised and a bit humbled, having expected nothing new and admitting the confident planners had focused on the slides.

qa.q: Which approach could Sachin keep using after the demo, and why?
qa.a: Sachin could keep the silent-writing round before every big release, since it draws out risks from people who stay quiet in stand-ups.

qa.q: How might Ritu feel on seeing the team test Ritu's concern that night?
qa.a: Ritu may feel heard and more confident, since a worry Ritu might never have voiced aloud is being taken seriously.

grounding: It shows a team lead running a short private pre-mortem before a client demo, which surfaces loading and login risks the confident planners missed.
